title: MCP Configuration, Authentication & Secrets
scopeHtml: Scope: MCP server scope and permissions, authentication patterns by service type, secret storage and rotation, and what regulated customers add.

notes.title: MCP scopes and permissions
notes.html:
The idea. An MCP server config lives at a scope: local (you, this project), project (a committed .mcp.json, shared with everyone who clones), user (you, every project), managed (admin-controlled). Permission rules can name a single tool by server and tool name, so you can allow get_issue without allowing every tool on the server.

Real life. A Wi-Fi password: on a sticky note on your own desk (local), on the office wall (project), in your password manager (user), or pushed by IT (managed).

Tech. Per-repo, per-user and system-wide git config.

notes.title: Authentication patterns
notes.html:
The idea. The right mechanism depends on where the service runs and whose identity is used.

Service Pattern
Remote, user identity (SaaS) OAuth: server returns 401, client opens a browser sign-in, token issued and stored
Remote, service identity API key via an environment variable
Local, file access stdio, no network auth; filesystem permissions are the boundary
GitHub MCP example personal access token passed as a header

Real life. Hotel: a key card tied to you (OAuth), a staff master key kept in a safe (service key), and a door that is just physically in your own house (stdio).

Tech. "Sign in with Google" vs. a service account key vs. a unix file permission.

notes.title: Secrets
notes.html:
The idea. Three practices keep a credential from leaking.

  1. Separation. The config holds a variable reference; the value lives elsewhere.
  2. A home for the value. An environment variable injected at execution, or a secret store when several people or services need it.
  3. Rotation. On a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.

A committed key stays in git history and in every clone, so deleting the line is not a fix; you must rotate. Scope each credential narrowly and keep a record of who uses it.

Real life. You lose a house key. Hiding the keyring does not help; you change the lock.

Tech. AWS keys in a public repo are scraped within minutes.

notes.title: Regulated integrations
notes.html:
The idea. A regulated customer asks more than "does it connect?": who is the model acting as, where does data go, can an admin lock the setup, is every access logged?

  • Managed configuration answers "can a developer change auth?" (no).
  • A PostToolUse audit hook answers "is every call logged?" (yes, deterministically, regardless of the model).
  • A region-pinned HTTP endpoint plus a matching platform answers "where does data go?".

Real life. A bank vault: CCTV that cannot be switched off by the teller (hook), keys held by the head office (managed config), a vault located in the right country (residency).

Tech. Audit logging at the API gateway rather than trusting each service to log.

questions.promptHtml:
A teammate wants an MCP server config shared with everyone who clones the repo. Which scope?

  • A. Local scope
  • B. Project scope (a committed .mcp.json)
  • C. User scope
  • D. Managed scope only

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Project scope writes the server configuration into a file in the repo; local is you in one project; user is you across projects; managed is admin-controlled.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Permission rules can target a single MCP tool by server and tool name, so you can allow get_issue without allowing every tool on the server.

questions.promptHtml:
Match the pattern. A cloud SaaS MCP server where the user's own identity is part of authorization.

  • A. API key in a committed config file
  • B. OAuth: the server returns 401, the client opens a browser sign-in, a token is issued and stored
  • C. stdio with no auth
  • D. A shared password in the system prompt

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. User identity on a remote service → OAuth; service identity on a remote service → API key via environment variable; local filesystem service → stdio where filesystem permissions are the boundary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Remote + user identity → OAuth (401 triggers a browser sign-in; no secret is hand-copied). Remote + service identity → API key injected via environment variable, never committed. Local + file access → stdio, where filesystem permissions are the boundary and a settings deny rule is the governance layer. Committed keys (A) and prompt-embedded passwords (D) are exposures.

questions.contextHtml: A developer put an API key inline in a project-scope MCP config to "get it working", committed it, and pushed. They notice a day later, delete the key from the file and push again.
questions.promptHtml:
Is the incident closed?

  • A. Yes, the key is no longer in the current files
  • B. No: it remains in repository history and in every clone, so rotate it immediately, move the new key to an environment variable or secret store referenced by name, and scope it narrowly
  • C. Yes, if the repo is private
  • D. No, but only a new branch is required

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deleting the line and moving on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who had read access? Was it a service or user credential? What can the key reach?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke and rotate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Exposure through history, forks, CI logs, caches.
  4. How I'd verify each: Audit key usage logs for the exposure window.
  5. Root cause: A value travelled with the configuration that references it.
  6. Fix: Config holds a variable reference; value lives in the environment (CI secret) or a secret manager.
  7. Prevention: Secret scanning pre-commit, narrow scopes, a registry of which services use which credential.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on rewriting history as the only fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Why can't you rotate a baked-in value cleanly? → The old value stays in history and every consumer hard-coded to it breaks on change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes the line.
  • Hire: rotates.
  • Strong hire: rotates, restructures, adds scanning and least privilege.

questions.promptHtml:
An auditor asks for a deterministic record of every tool call and its parameters, plus assurance developers cannot change the auth setup. Which pair of controls answers this?

  • A. A longer CLAUDE.md and a warning comment
  • B. A PostToolUse audit hook (fires regardless of model decisions) and an administrator-deployed managed configuration that users cannot override
  • C. A prompt asking Claude to log its actions
  • D. User-level settings in every laptop

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Hooks are deterministic; managed config is non-overridable; add a region-pinned endpoint to answer "where does data go?".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A PostToolUse hook fires deterministically for every call regardless of what the model decides, so the audit log cannot be skipped. A managed configuration deployed by an administrator cannot be overridden by users, so auth setup is consistent. A prompt (C) is a request, not a control; user-level settings (D) are editable by each developer.

questions.promptHtml:
Which scope applies an MCP server only to you, in one project?

  • A. Project
  • B. Local
  • C. User
  • D. Managed

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Local is you in this project; user is you in all projects; project is shared via the repo; managed is admin-controlled.

questions.promptHtml:
You want Claude to use get_issue on a GitHub server but never delete_repo. What do you do?

  • A. Don't connect the server
  • B. Write permission rules that name the specific MCP tool by server and tool name
  • C. Trust the model
  • D. Use bypass mode

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Rules can target a single MCP tool, not only the whole server.

sections.label: Deep explanation

questions.promptHtml:
What triggers the OAuth flow with a remote MCP server?

  • A. A pasted password
  • B. The server returns 401 Unauthorized; the client starts a browser sign-in and stores the issued token
  • C. An environment variable
  • D. A file permission

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. No one copies a secret by hand.

sections.label: Deep explanation

questions.promptHtml:
A CI pipeline using the Agent SDK needs a credential. Where does it come from?

  • A. Hard-coded in code
  • B. Injected as a secret by the pipeline runner into an environment variable
  • C. Committed to config
  • D. Typed by a developer each run

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The key identifies the service account and lives only in the environment at execution.

questions.promptHtml:
For a local stdio MCP server accessing files, what is the security boundary?

  • A. A network firewall
  • B. The filesystem permission model, with a settings deny rule as the governance layer
  • C. OAuth
  • D. TLS

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. There is no network authentication on stdio.

questions.promptHtml:
Where should an API key referenced by an MCP config live?

  • A. Inline in the config for convenience
  • B. In an environment variable or secret store, with the config holding only a reference
  • C. In CLAUDE.md
  • D. In the system prompt

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Configs get committed, shared and cloned; a value written inline rides along.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "secrets". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
Why is rotation the only correct response to a leaked key?

  • A. Rotation is faster
  • B. An exposed key cannot be made secret again, and a value baked into committed code cannot be cleaned out of history
  • C. It is a policy
  • D. It reduces cost

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Code that reads from env or a secret store rotates without changing the code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "secrets". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
When is a secret store preferable to a plain environment variable?

  • A. For a one-off local script
  • B. When several services or people need the credential, so one rotation updates every consumer and reads are recorded
  • C. Never
  • D. When the secret is short

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It centralizes the value and removes copies in each service's own files.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "secrets". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
What habit limits the damage from a leaked integration key?

  • A. One master key for all integrations
  • B. Scope each credential to the narrowest access its task needs and record who uses it
  • C. Share keys in chat
  • D. Long key names

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. A compromised key then reaches only what that integration required.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "secrets". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
An auditor asks where data goes. Which combination gives a checkable answer?

  • A. A verbal assurance
  • B. An HTTP endpoint in a specific region combined with a platform deployment pinned to that region
  • C. A longer prompt
  • D. A global endpoint

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. This is why platform choice matters at audit time, not just build time.
